Graph Processing & Analytics for Relational Databases

Apache AGE is an extension for PostgreSQL that enables users to leverage a graph database on top of the existing relational databases. AGE is an acronym for A Graph Extension and is inspired by Bitnine's AgensGraph, a multi-model database fork of PostgreSQL. The basic principle of the project is to create a single storage that handles both the relational and graph data model so that the users can use the standard ANSI SQL along with openCypher, one of the most popular graph query languages today. There is a strong need for cohesive, easy-to-implement multi-model databases. As an extension of PostgreSQL, AGE supports all the functionalities and features of PostgreSQL while also offering a graph model to boot.
Refer to our latest Apache AGE documentation to learn about installation, features, built-in functions, and Cypher queries.
You can use a package management that your OS provides to download PostgreSQL.

You can download the Postgres source code and install your own instance of Postgres. You can read instructions on how to install from source code for different versions on the official Postgres Website.
Clone the github repository or download the <a href="https://github.com/apache/age/releases">download an official release.

Ardent models use Laravel's built-in Validator class. Defining validation rules for a model is simple and is typically done in your model class as a static variable:

> **Note**: you're free to use the array syntax for validation rules as well. _I hope you don't mind the old Laravel docs link, but as good as Laravel documentation is, clear reference on pipe/array syntaxes for Validation rules is unfortunately gone since 5.1._
> **Note:** Ardent leverages Laravel's MessagesBag object which has a simple and elegant method of formatting errors.
Just like the Laravel Validator, Ardent lets you set custom error messages using the same syntax.
You can create custom validation rules the same way you would for the Laravel Validator.
For example, you may use `beforeSave` to hash a users password (actually, it would be a better idea to use auto-hashing!):
- `name`, `type` and `id`, used by `morphTo`, `morphOne` and `morphMany` (the last two requires `name` to be defined)
> **Note:** This feature was based on the easy relations on Yii 1.1 ActiveRecord.

Believe it or not, the code above performs essentially the same task as its older, albeit rather verbose sibling. Ardent populates the model object with attributes from user submitted form data. No more hair-pulling trying to find out which Eloquent property you've forgotten to populate. Let Ardent take care of the boring stuff, while you get on with the fun stuffs!
It follows the same mass assignment rules internally, depending on the `$fillable`/`$guarded` properties.

Ardent will automatically replace the plain-text password attribute with secure hash checksum and save it to database. It uses the Laravel `Hash::make()` method internally to generate hash. _Note: It's advised to use Eloquent's `$hidden` attribute so the password, even hashed, won't come out that easily if you're building an API or similar :)_

Approved `teardown` removes what golive created; backups and any restore remain manual, supervised work.
`golive teardown` plans the removal, deletes only what golive provably created (ownership proofs and
`--confirm-destroy`), and re-reads the DNS zone's golive-owned record list and the host's own
project read after deleting. Nothing it cannot remove is dropped silently: a leftover — an
unreadable zone, an unremovable host project, a provider that is not signed in — becomes a handoff
naming what remains and the exact fix, and Supabase/Neon projects and the Resend sending domain
(#9). A removal forgets the baseline golive
recorded for that resource, so `golive status` does not report golive's own teardown as drift, and
a sending key golive revoked is reported as a warning instead of a pass, because the provider
offers no read to confirm it.

refuses without the approved plan id and `--yes`. Changing the installed release invalidates old
approvals. DNS, live-payment and deletion steps have extra gates (`--confirm-dns`,
`--confirm-live`, `--confirm-destroy`), and a project's first production deploy needs
`--confirm-live` as well, because approving a plan alone used to be enough to write production for

dialog can save a needed API key; your own editor is the fallback. Keys live in
`~/.config/golive/credentials`, a local plaintext file at mode 0600 outside your app repo — not an
OS keychain, so anything running as your user can read it. The execution code keeps values out of
argv, plans, state, reports and command output, storing fingerprints instead of values.
`golive credentials --remove NAME --yes` deletes one stored entry, irreversibly; revoking the
token at the provider is what actually ends access. Mac login passwords stay with macOS/vendor
authentication prompts; GoLive never asks you to enter one in its key dialog. The full boundary is
whole-bundle updates and local rollback; automatic replacement is off by default. Update between
deployment runs, never between a plan and its apply. Cloud resources are unaffected by rollback.

Settings merge in this order: built-in defaults, `ruvio.toml` (template: `ruvio.example.toml`), `RUVIO_*` environment variables, then CLI flags. The file is read once, at process start. See Configuration.

These commands run on the shard that owns the key. `examples/09_building_blocks_tour.py` runs the main ones in a few seconds against a local server; the use cases page shows each job with all six clients. A key that never uses them stores nothing extra. `GET`, `SET`, and `INCR` do not consult them.
|Command|What it replaces a second system for|

|`LEASE` / `RELEASE`|A fencing token for one key. The shard is the holder. Tokens only grow: after expiry, `RELEASE`, `DEL`, a restart, a failover or a slot move, the next grant is larger. The grant is a WAL record. `GET` of a lease is `WRONGTYPE`.|

|`SEMAPHORE` / `RELEASE`|At most N holders at once, each with its own TTL. A crashed holder frees its slot when its TTL passes. The first holder stays in the object; each further holder is 16 bytes. The key goes away with the last one.|
|`RENEW`|Extends a `LEASE` or `SEMAPHORE` holder by its token without releasing it, so a long job keeps its slot and its fencing token.|
|`INCRBY ... MAX`|A counter that never passes a capacity. A refused call returns nil and changes nothing, so no compensating `DECR`.|

|`SETV`|A conditional string write. The call succeeds only when the caller still has the current version, so two clients cannot both turn 12 into 11. The version exists only on keys written with `SETV`.|

|`CHANGES`|`CHANGES START` arms an in-memory feed of later `SET`, `SETV`, `LEASE`, and `RELEASE` notes on that shard. Nothing is recorded before `START`. The feed is not the WAL, and it is empty after restart.|

|`XADD DELAY`|The stream entry is stored now. `XREADGROUP` skips it until the delay passes. `XREAD` can still see it. The hold is a WAL record and a snapshot trailer, and it is written only when a delay is set.|
|`SET ... IFEQ` / `IFGT` / `IFLT`, `DELEX ... IFEQ`|A compare-and-set, a watermark that only moves forward or a delete that checks the value, without a script. A refused call writes nothing.|
|`ZPOPBYSCORE` / `ZMOVEDUE`|Take the due members of a sorted set, or move them to a list, in one command: the due-job queue without a scheduler.|
|`LPUSHCAP` / `RPUSHCAP`|Push to a list and trim it to a length in one call: a capped recent-items list.|
|`RUVIO HOTKEYS` / `RUVIO BIGKEYS`|Which keys take the traffic and which values are large, sampled; off unless `key_stats` is on.|
|`LIMIT`|A fixed-window, sliding-window or token-bucket rate limit in one call, with fixed state per key. A refused call writes nothing.|
|`IDEM`|Request de-duplication on the shard that owns the key: `BEGIN` tells a caller to run, wait or conflict, and a repeat of a finished request gets the saved result.|
|`FILLGET` / `FILLSET`|One caller refills a missing or stale cache entry while the others get `BUSY` or the stale value. The markers live in memory only.|
|`TRANSFER`|Moves an amount between two integer strings of one slot in one WAL record, with an optional cap on the destination.|
|`CHANGES SUBSCRIBE`|A resumable push stream of this shard's WAL, with a cursor to continue from after a disconnect or restart.|
|`JSON.INDEX`|A field index over JSON documents with a key prefix, so a lookup by field does not scan.|
|`CLIENT DURABILITY`|Holds this connection's replies until `n` replicas have the writes on disk; `ruvio coordinator` fails over only to a replica that has them.|

|**Against Redis 8.10.2**|59 of 60 commands at or above 0.97×, geometric mean 1.22×|4-core Azure x86 VM, one shard, `memory` durability, 50 clients, pipeline 16, 64-byte values, five alternating rounds (2026-10-11)|

First-party clients speak RESP2, do not send `CLIENT SETINFO`, and learn `CLUSTER SLOTS` from one seed address. Guides: Clients · `clients/`.

The .NET integration packages provide an `IDistributedCache` provider, ASP.NET Core output caching and Data Protection key-ring storage, plus opt-in rate limiting, HTTP idempotency and distributed locks. They are separate packages; existing server commands and applications that do not enable them incur no new per-key feature state.

Native `IDEM` adds atomic reservation, ownership checks, fingerprint conflicts and binary result replay for any RESP client. The ASP.NET Core idempotency package uses this command, not Lua. `ONCE` remains the simpler TTL marker. Retention and durability bound deduplication; external side effects still require their own transaction/idempotency mechanism.

The differences are about ownership, the durability contract, and how much of the Redis surface is implemented. Measured results are in Performance. How a Ruvio process runs is on How it runs.
|Wire|RESP2/3, full surface|Redis and Memcached|Redis-compatible|RESP2 subset, listed in CI|
|Hot path|Shared engine, I/O threads|Single-node throughput|Separate string and object stores|One owner per shard, no lock on apply|
|Cluster|Bus, migration, failover|Its own scale story|Cluster-capable store|Static 16,384 slots, misrouted keys forwarded; automatic failover of a primary and its replicas with `ruvio coordinator`|

|Keep the other when|You need modules, the full Sentinel feature set, or a command Ruvio does not list|You want that single-node scale claim|You want a .NET stack and Tsavorite as the store|The written subset and the shard contract are enough|

Projects allow for the repository to maintain different mappings for different compare objectives. This allows a central pgCompare repository to be used for multiple compare projects. Each table has a `pid` column which is the project id. If no project is specified, the default project (pid = 1) is used.

Properties are categorized into four sections: system, repository, source, and target. Each section has specific properties, as described in detail in the documentation. The properties can be specified via a configuration file, environment variables or a combination of both. To use environment variables, the environment variable will be the name of the property in upper case with dashes '-' converted to underscore '_' and prefixed with PGCOMPARE_. For example, batch-fetch-size can be set by using the environment variable PGCOMPARE_BATCH_FETCH_SIZE.
